questions.question: What is the principal intermolecular force that must be overcome when hexane ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$, BP $=69^\circ$C) is vaporised?
questions.answer: Hexane is a non-polar hydrocarbon, so the only intermolecular forces between its molecules are dispersion forces (temporary dipole–induced dipole forces). These are overcome on vaporisation; the covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken.

questions.question: In which one of the following would the position of equilibrium not be affected by a volume change at constant temperature?
questions.answer: A change in volume (and so pressure) only shifts the position of equilibrium if the number of moles of gas differs between the two sides. In D there are 2 mol of gas on each side, so the position is unaffected. A (3 mol vs 2 mol), B (1 vs 2) and C (1 vs 2) are all affected.

questions.question: How many different compounds have the formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$?
questions.answer: The structural isomers of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ are pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: 3 compounds.

questions.question: The solubility of magnesium chloride ($\text{MgCl}_2$) may be represented as $X$ mol L$^{-1}$. Which expression may be used to determine the solubility product, $K_{sp}$, for magnesium chloride?
questions.answer: $\text{MgCl}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$: $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]=X$ and $[\text{Cl}^-]=2X$, so $K_{sp}=X(2X)^2=4X^3$.

questions.question: What is the pH of a $0.20$ M solution of sodium benzoate, $\text{Na}(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO})$? The $K_a$ of benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is $6.5\times10^{-5}$.
questions.answer:
The benzoate ion is a weak base: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}+\text{OH}^-$.
$$K_b=\frac{K_w}{K_a}=\frac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{6.5\times10^{-5}}=1.54\times10^{-10}$$
$$[\text{OH}^-]=\sqrt{K_b\times0.20}=\sqrt{3.1\times10^{-11}}=5.55\times10^{-6}\ \text{M}\Rightarrow pOH=5.26,\ pH=8.74.$$

questions.question: Methanoic acid and ethanoic acid are both weak acids with the following $K_a$ values: methanoic acid (HCOOH) $1.82\times10^{-4}$; ethanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) $1.74\times10^{-5}$. Two separate solutions were prepared, one of $0.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ methanoic acid and the other of $0.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ ethanoic acid. Which one of the following would be present at the highest concentration at $25^\circ$C?
questions.answer: Both acids are weak and so are mostly undissociated, so the ions have much lower concentrations than the molecules. Ethanoic acid is the weaker acid (smaller $K_a$), so more of it remains undissociated: $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]\approx0.0987$ M compared with $[\text{HCOOH}]\approx0.096$ M. The highest concentration is $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.
options: HCOOH in the methanoic acid solution

questions.question: Two chemical reactions occur as follows: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3+X\rightarrow$ 2-chloropentane; 2-chloropentane + sodium hydroxide solution $\rightarrow Y$. $X$ and $Y$ are given by:
questions.answer: Adding HCl across the C=C bond of pent-1-ene gives 2-chloropentane (Markovnikov addition); $\text{Cl}_2$ would give a dichloro compound. Aqueous NaOH then substitutes OH for Cl on the same carbon, giving pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$.

questions.question:
The following table shows the value of the autoionisation constant of pure water at various temperatures and at a constant pressure.

| Temperature ($^\circ$C) | 0 | 25 | 50 | 75 | 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_w$ | $1.1\times10^{-15}$ | $1.0\times10^{-14}$ | $5.5\times10^{-14}$ | $2.0\times10^{-13}$ | $5.6\times10^{-13}$ |

Given this data, which one of the following statements about pure water is correct?
questions.answer: $K_w=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{OH}^-]$ increases with temperature, so autoionisation is endothermic and more ions form: $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{OH}^-]=\sqrt{K_w}$ both increase. The pH $=-\log[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ therefore decreases (e.g. 6.14 at $100^\circ$C), but pure water remains neutral since $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{OH}^-]$.
options: The $[\text{OH}^-]$ will decrease with increasing temperature.
The $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ will increase with increasing temperature.
Its pH will increase with increasing temperature.
Its pH will always be exactly 7 at any temperature.

questions.question:
The UV-visible spectrum of a certain compound is shown (absorbance against wavelength, with a strong peak near $255$ nm and a smaller peak near $400$ nm). Consider the following statements about this compound and its UV-visible spectrum:

I. The amount of light absorbed by a solution of this compound depends on its concentration.
II. The amount of light absorbed by a solution of this compound depends on the wavelength of light used.
III. The spectrum is a result of electrons falling back from higher to lower electron energy levels.
IV. The concentration of a solution of this compound can only be determined by UV-visible spectroscopy at 250 nm.

Which of the following statements are true?
questions.answer: I is true (absorbance is proportional to concentration, the Beer–Lambert law) and II is true (the spectrum shows absorbance varying with wavelength). III is false: absorption occurs when electrons are promoted from lower to higher energy levels (emission occurs as they fall back). IV is false: the concentration can be determined at any wavelength at which the compound absorbs (such as 400 nm), though the strongest absorption gives the best sensitivity.

questions.question: If Solution X has a pH of 3 and Solution Y has a pH of 6, we can conclude that
questions.answer: $[\text{H}^+]=10^{-pH}$: $[\text{H}^+]_X=10^{-3}$ M and $[\text{H}^+]_Y=10^{-6}$ M, so X has $1000$ times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y. (The $[\text{OH}^-]$ in Y is $1000$ times that in X, and a lower pH does not by itself show a stronger acid, because concentration also matters.)
options: $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution X is 1000 times that of $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution Y.
$[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution X is half that of $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution Y.
$[\text{OH}^-]$ in Solution Y is twice that of $[\text{OH}^-]$ in Solution X.
Solution Y must contain a stronger acid than Solution X.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M HCl and $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solutions is true?
questions.answer: Both acids are monoprotic with the same amount ($1.0\times10^{-3}$ mol), so each is exactly neutralised by $1.0\times10^{-3}$ mol of NaOH ($10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M) regardless of strength. HCl is a strong acid (fully ionised) and has a higher $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, conductivity and reaction rate with magnesium than the weak acid $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, so A, B and D are false.
options: Each solution will have the same electrical conductivity.
Each solution will react at the same rate with 1.00 g of magnesium ribbon.
Each solution will react completely with $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M NaOH solution.
The concentration of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions will be greater in the $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solution.

questions.question: The indicator HIn is used in a titration between hydrochloric acid and magnesium hydroxide solutions. The following equation represents how the indicator works: $\text{HIn}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{In}^-(aq)$ (green; purple). The indicator is added to $20.0$ mL of magnesium hydroxide solution in a conical flask and the hydrochloric acid is added via a burette until the end point is observed. The acidic and basic solutions are of similar concentrations and the flask is swirled continuously as the acid is added. Which one of the following statements describes the expected observations for the colour of the solution in the conical flask?
questions.answer: In the basic $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ solution the indicator equilibrium lies to the right (low $[\text{H}^+]$), so the solution starts purple ($\text{In}^-$) and turns green (HIn) when the solution becomes acidic. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2+2\text{HCl}\rightarrow\text{MgCl}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$: each mole of base needs 2 mol of HCl, so with similar concentrations about twice the volume is required, approximately $40$ mL.
options: solution starts green and turns purple after the addition of approximately 10 mL
solution starts green and turns purple after the addition of approximately 40 mL
solution starts purple and turns green after the addition of approximately 10 mL
solution starts purple and turns green after the addition of approximately 40 mL

questions.question: Which of the following compounds forms a $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ aqueous solution with a pH closest to 7.00?
questions.answer: Ethanol is a neutral molecule that does not ionise appreciably in water, so its solution has a pH very close to 7. Sodium ethanoate is a basic salt (pH about 8.9), ethanamine is a weak base (pH about 11.8) and 2,3-dihydroxypropanoic acid is a weak carboxylic acid (pH about 2.4).

questions.question: The halogenation of 2-methylbut-2-ene with iodine will produce:
questions.answer: Iodine adds across the C=C bond of 2-methylbut-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$, putting one I on each of the two double-bond carbons (carbons 2 and 3 of the butane chain): 2,3-diiodo-2-methylbutane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CI}-\text{CHICH}_3$.

questions.question: Which of the following will decrease $[\text{Cl}^-]$ in a saturated solution of $\text{PbCl}_2$? I. Addition of a small amount of water. II. Addition of a small amount of $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$.
questions.answer: In a saturated solution (with undissolved solid present) the concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ is fixed by $K_{sp}$, so adding a small amount of water just dissolves a little more solid and $[\text{Cl}^-]$ is unchanged (I does not decrease it). Adding $\text{AgNO}_3$ precipitates $\text{AgCl}$: $\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{AgCl}(s)$, which removes $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, decreasing $[\text{Cl}^-]$ (II).

questions.question: What is the correct systematic name for the compound shown? (The structure has a carbon skeleton $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, drawn with the two ethyl groups on either side.)
questions.answer: The longest continuous carbon chain runs through both ethyl groups and contains 6 carbons (hexane), with a methyl branch on each of carbons 3 and 4: 3,4-dimethylhexane. (Choosing a shorter main chain, as in the other names, is incorrect.)

questions.question: Propanone ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$) can be made from propan-2-ol using a copper–zinc catalyst: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}(g)+\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-54$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. At equilibrium at a particular temperature, $10\%$ of the propan-2-ol is converted to propanone. In order to increase the percentage yield of propanone at equilibrium, you should
questions.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H<0$), so lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (the exothermic direction). The forward reaction produces 2 mol of gas from 1 mol, so lowering the pressure favours the side with more moles of gas, the products. Both changes increase the yield of propanone.
options: lower the temperature and lower the pressure.
lower the temperature and raise the pressure.
raise the temperature and lower the pressure.
raise the temperature and raise the pressure.

questions.question: When propan-2-ol reacts to form an equilibrium mixture with propanone and hydrogen, which one of the following best represents how the rates of the forward and backward reactions change over time? (Each graph plots rate against time for the forward reaction $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}\rightarrow\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}+\text{H}_2$ and the reverse reaction.)
questions.answer: Starting with only propan-2-ol, the forward rate is initially at its maximum and decreases as the reactant is used up, while the reverse rate starts at zero (no products) and increases as products form. At equilibrium the two rates become equal and remain constant. This is shown only in graph D, where the falling forward curve and the rising reverse curve meet at a common constant rate (the other graphs either start the reverse reaction at a high rate or do not show the two rates becoming equal).

questions.question: The structure of oxalic acid is shown ($\text{HOOC}-\text{COOH}$, a diprotic acid). A $25.0$ mL solution of oxalic acid reacts completely with $15.0$ mL of $2.50$ M NaOH. The concentration of the oxalic acid solution is
questions.answer: $n(\text{NaOH})=2.50\times0.0150=0.0375$ mol. Oxalic acid has two acidic hydrogens, so $n(\text{oxalic acid})=0.0375/2=0.01875$ mol and $c=\dfrac{0.01875}{0.0250}=0.750$ M.

questions.question: A $20.0$ mL aliquot of a solution of sodium propanoate ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COONa}$) was titrated with a standardised $0.1042$ M solution of HCl. The titre volume was $21.20$ mL. The $pK_a$ of propanoic acid is $4.87$. Which of the following is closest to the pH at the equivalence point?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{HCl})=0.1042\times0.02120=2.209\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{propanoic acid})$ formed. Total volume $=41.20$ mL, so $[\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]=\dfrac{2.209\times10^{-3}}{0.04120}=0.0536$ M. $K_a=10^{-4.87}=1.35\times10^{-5}$, so
$$[\text{H}^+]=\sqrt{K_a\times0.0536}=8.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}\Rightarrow pH=3.07,$$
closest to 3.08.

questions.question:
In an experiment, $1.0$ mol of pure phosgene, $\text{COCl}_2$, is placed in a $3.0$ L flask where the following reaction takes place: $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $K_{eq}=2.1\times10^{-8}$.

It can be assumed that, at equilibrium, the amount of unreacted $\text{COCl}_2$ is approximately equal to $1.0$ mol. On the basis of the data provided, explain why this assumption is justified.
questions.answer: The equilibrium constant is extremely small ($2.1\times10^{-8}$), so the equilibrium lies very far to the left: only a tiny amount of $\text{COCl}_2$ decomposes to form $\text{CO}$ and $\text{Cl}_2$. The amount of $\text{COCl}_2$ that reacts is negligible compared with the $1.0$ mol initially present, so (to two significant figures) the amount of $\text{COCl}_2$ at equilibrium is still approximately $1.0$ mol.

questions.question:
In an experiment, $1.0$ mol of pure phosgene, $\text{COCl}_2$, is placed in a $3.0$ L flask where the following reaction takes place: $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $K_{eq}=2.1\times10^{-8}$.

Calculate the equilibrium concentration, in mol L$^{-1}$, of carbon monoxide, CO. Assume that the amount of unreacted $\text{COCl}_2$ is approximately equal to $1.0$ mol.
questions.answer:
$[\text{COCl}_2]=\dfrac{1.0}{3.0}=0.333$ M. From the equation, $[\text{CO}]=[\text{Cl}_2]=y$.
$$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{COCl}_2]}=\frac{y^2}{0.333}=2.1\times10^{-8}$$
$$y=\sqrt{2.1\times10^{-8}\times0.333}=8.4\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$
So $[\text{CO}]=8.4\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$, which is very small compared with $0.333$ M, confirming the assumption.

questions.question:
In an experiment, $1.0$ mol of pure phosgene, $\text{COCl}_2$, is placed in a $3.0$ L flask where the following reaction takes place: $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $K_{eq}=2.1\times10^{-8}$.

What is the equilibrium concentration of chlorine gas?
questions.answer: $\text{CO}$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ are produced in equal amounts (1 : 1), so $[\text{Cl}_2]=[\text{CO}]=8.4\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: In an experiment, carbon monoxide and chlorine were placed in a sealed flask and allowed to reach equilibrium, forming phosgene: $\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{COCl}_2(g)$. The temperature, pressure and volume were initially the same as in an experiment where, for $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $K_{eq}=2.1\times10^{-8}$. What is the equilibrium constant for this reaction?
questions.answer:
This is the reverse of the original reaction at the same temperature, so $K$ is inverted:
$$K_{eq}=\frac1{2.1\times10^{-8}}=4.8\times10^{7}.$$

questions.question:
The graph shows how the concentrations of reactants and products vary with time for $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{Cl}_2(g)+\text{CO}(g)$, $\Delta H=+108$ kJ, in a closed vessel.

Identify the changes applied to the equilibrium at time $=10$ minutes and at time $=14$ minutes.
questions.answer:
At $t=10$ min: $\text{CO}$ was removed from the equilibrium (its concentration drops suddenly, and the system shifts right to partly replace it).

At $t=14$ min: the volume of the container was increased (by about one third), which reduces the concentrations of all gases at once (the system then shifts towards the side with more moles of gas).

questions.question:
The graph shows how the concentrations of reactants and products vary with time for $\text{COCl}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{Cl}_2(g)+\text{CO}(g)$, $\Delta H=+108$ kJ, in a closed vessel.

Explain, using collision theory, the reason for the change at time $=4$ minutes.
questions.answer: At $t=4$ min the concentrations of the products ($\text{CO}$ and $\text{Cl}_2$) gradually increase while that of $\text{COCl}_2$ decreases, with no sudden step: the temperature was increased. The forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H=+108$ kJ), so it has the higher activation energy. A temperature increase increases the proportion of particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy for both reactions, but the increase is greater for the endothermic (higher activation energy) forward reaction. There are therefore more successful collisions per second for the forward reaction than for the reverse, so the forward rate increases more than the reverse rate and the equilibrium shifts to the right until the rates are equal again, with a greater proportion of products than before.

questions.question:
At a particular temperature, a saturated aqueous solution of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ has $pH=12.40$.

What is the concentration of hydroxide ions in this solution?

At a particular temperature, a saturated aqueous solution of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ has $pH=12.40$.

What is the $K_{sp}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ at this temperature?
questions.answer:
$\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$, so $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]=\tfrac12[\text{OH}^-]=0.5\times0.0251=0.0126$ M.
$$K_{sp}=[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2=(0.0126)(0.0251)^2=7.9\times10^{-6}$$
(7.8 × 10⁻⁶ if the rounded value 0.025 M is used).

questions.question:
At a particular temperature, a saturated aqueous solution of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ has $pH=12.40$.

A sample of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is suspended in $100.0$ mL of water. The mixture is stirred vigorously and $3$ M sulfuric acid is added dropwise to it while monitoring the pH of the solution. At the point that the pH reaches $7.0$, there is solid calcium sulfate suspended in the solution. Write an equation for the reaction of sulfuric acid and calcium hydroxide. Explain why calcium sulfate solid, but not calcium hydroxide, is present when the pH reaches $7.0$.
questions.answer:
$$\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)+\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)\rightarrow\text{CaSO}_4(s)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
At pH 7 all of the hydroxide ions from the calcium hydroxide have been neutralised by the sulfuric acid (a pH of 7 means no excess $\text{OH}^-$ remains), so no solid calcium hydroxide is left. The resulting solution contains $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions, but calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble, so it forms a precipitate and is present as a solid. Since it is the salt of a strong acid and a strong base, it is neutral and does not react further with water to change the pH.

questions.question:
Some rocks were thought to consist of insoluble silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) and calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$). The fraction of $\text{CaCO}_3$ in an $8.64$ g sample of the crushed rock was determined by mixing the sample with excess hydrochloric acid: $2\text{HCl}(aq)+\text{CaCO}_3(s)\rightarrow\text{CaCl}_2(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+\text{CO}_2(g)$. The resulting solution was filtered and the $\text{SiO}_2$ that was collected was washed and dried. The mass of $\text{SiO}_2$ was found to be $1.55$ g.

Calculate the expected percentage of $\text{CaCO}_3$ in the original rock sample.
questions.answer:
The $\text{SiO}_2$ does not react, so the mass of $\text{CaCO}_3$ is $8.64-1.55=7.09$ g.
$$\%\ \text{CaCO}_3=\frac{7.09}{8.64}\times100=82.1\%.$$

questions.question: Some rocks were thought to consist of insoluble silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) and calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$). An $8.64$ g sample of crushed rock was mixed with excess hydrochloric acid ($2\text{HCl}+\text{CaCO}_3\rightarrow\text{CaCl}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$) and filtered. To check the result, excess ammonium oxalate solution was added to the filtered solution. The calcium ions present precipitate as $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$ was collected by filtration, washed and dried. It was then heated to convert it to $\text{CaO}$ and a mass of $3.87$ g was obtained. Calculate the percentage of $\text{CaCO}_3$ in the rock sample from this data.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{CaO})=\dfrac{3.87}{56.1}=0.0690$ mol. All the calcium originates from the $\text{CaCO}_3$ (one $\text{Ca}$ per formula unit throughout), so $n(\text{CaCO}_3)=0.0690$ mol.

$m(\text{CaCO}_3)=0.0690\times100.1=6.91$ g.
$$\%\ \text{CaCO}_3=\frac{6.91}{8.64}\times100=79.9\%.$$
(This is slightly lower than the $82.1\%$ from part (a); the difference suggests the silica was not completely pure or that the dried residue contained a little other insoluble material.)

questions.question:
Industrially, ethanol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, is made by either of two methods. One method uses ethene (ethylene), $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, which is derived from crude oil. The other method uses a sugar such as sucrose, $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$, and yeast in aqueous solution. The production of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ from $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$ and yeast proceeds according to $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow4\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+4\text{CO}_2(g)$.

Determine the mass, in grams, of pure $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ that would be produced from $1.25$ kg of $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$ dissolved in water.
questions.answer:
$M(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11})=342.3$ g mol$^{-1}$: $n=\dfrac{1250}{342.3}=3.652$ mol. From the equation, $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=4\times3.652=14.61$ mol, and $M(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=46.07$ g mol$^{-1}$:
$$m=14.61\times46.07=673\ \text{g}.$$

questions.question: Ethanol can be made industrially from ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ (derived from crude oil). How is ethanol derived from ethene? Include a balanced equation in your response and identify the type of reaction.
questions.answer:
Ethanol is manufactured by reacting ethene with steam (water) in the presence of a dilute strong acid catalyst (e.g. phosphoric acid):
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\overset{\text{dil. strong acid}}{\rightleftharpoons}\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(g)$$
The reaction is an addition (hydration) reaction: an H atom and an OH group add across the C=C double bond. The reaction is reversible, with only a small percentage of the ethene converted to ethanol per pass.

questions.question: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ can be converted into ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, in the presence of Reagent $X$. Identify Reagent $X$ and identify this type of reaction.
questions.answer: Reagent $X$ is an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium dichromate ($\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) or acidified potassium permanganate. The reaction is oxidation (of a primary alcohol, via ethanal, to a carboxylic acid).

questions.question: Ethanol is described as a primary alcohol. Draw the structure of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, classify it as a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol and explain your classification.
questions.answer:
Structure: a central carbon bonded to the $-$OH group and to three $-\text{CH}_3$ groups, i.e. $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OH}$:

```
        CH3
         |
CH3 --- C --- OH
         |
        CH3
```
2-methylpropan-2-ol is a **tertiary** alcohol, because the carbon atom bonded to the $-$OH group is itself bonded to three other carbon atoms (a primary alcohol's carbon is bonded to one other carbon, a secondary alcohol's to two).

questions.question: Describe how tertiary alcohols can be distinguished from primary and secondary alcohols in the laboratory.
questions.answer: Warm a sample of each alcohol with an acidified oxidising agent such as acidified potassium dichromate (orange) or acidified potassium permanganate (purple). Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised, so the dichromate changes from orange to green (or the permanganate decolourises from purple to colourless). Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised (the carbon bonded to the $-$OH has no hydrogen atom), so there is no colour change and the oxidising agent keeps its original colour.

questions.question: Outline the benefits and problems of using ethanol produced from sugars as a biofuel replacement for fuels based on petroleum.
questions.answer:
**Benefits:**

- Ethanol is renewable: it is made by fermenting sugars from crops that can be regrown quickly, whereas petroleum is non-renewable and takes millions of years to form.
- The $\text{CO}_2$ released when ethanol burns is offset by the $\text{CO}_2$ absorbed by the plants through photosynthesis as they grow, so the net impact on the greenhouse effect is lower than that of petrol (which releases carbon stored underground).
- Ethanol burns more cleanly than the components of petrol (its oxygen content means less carbon monoxide and particulates from incomplete combustion), and it avoids the environmental damage of drilling for oil.

**Problems:**

- Ethanol has a lower energy density than petrol (about 34% less energy per volume), so a larger volume of fuel is needed for the same energy.
- Growing crops for fuel uses arable land that could grow food, which can raise food prices and cause shortages, and may cause land clearing and loss of ecosystems.
- Most vehicles cannot run on 100% ethanol without modification.
- Production needs energy (for farming, transport, fermentation and distillation to separate ethanol from water), which makes it relatively expensive and reduces the carbon benefit.

questions.question:
A conductometric titration was carried out using $25.00$ mL of barium hydroxide and $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid. Conductivity measurements were recorded at five different intervals and the results plotted on the graph (conductivity against volume of acid added, from 22 to 34 mL; the measured points fall on two straight lines, one falling and one rising).

Using information from the graph, calculate the concentration of the barium hydroxide solution. Include a suitable chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer:
The conductivity is lowest at the equivalence point, where the lines of best fit through the falling and rising points intersect, at $29.0$ mL (±0.2 mL) of acid.
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)+\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4)=0.100\times0.0290=2.9\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2)$ (1 : 1).
$$c(\text{Ba(OH)}_2)=\frac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{0.02500}=0.116\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: A conductometric titration of $25.00$ mL of barium hydroxide with $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4+\text{Ba(OH)}_2\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) has an equivalence point at $29.0$ mL of acid. The titration was performed in a thermally insulated vessel. The sulfuric acid and barium hydroxide solutions were $20.2^\circ$C at the start of the titration. The enthalpy of neutralisation is $-57.6$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the final temperature of the solution when $40.0$ mL of the acid is added to $25.00$ mL of the base. (Take the specific heat capacity of the solution as $4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$ and its density as $1.00$ g mL$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
The barium hydroxide is the limiting reagent (the acid is in excess beyond $29.0$ mL), so the reaction is complete after $n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4)=n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2)=2.9\times10^{-3}$ mol, forming $n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=2\times2.9\times10^{-3}=5.8\times10^{-3}$ mol.

Energy released $=5.8\times10^{-3}\times57.6=0.334$ kJ $=334$ J.

Mass of solution $=25.00+40.0=65.0$ mL $\approx65.0$ g.
$$\Delta T=\frac{q}{mc}=\frac{334}{65.0\times4.18}=1.23^\circ\text{C}$$
$$T_{final}=20.2+1.23=21.4^\circ\text{C}.$$

questions.question:
A sample of an unknown metal salt is to be analysed. The cation in the metal salt is known to be one of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ or $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and the anion is known to be one of $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ or $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$. The metal salt is dissolved in water and the resulting colourless solution is divided into four equal samples to be tested, labelled A, B, C and D. The results of the tests are shown in the table. (Note: silver sulfate is soluble in dilute acid.)

| Sample | Test(s) conducted | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | A solution of NaOH is added. | A white precipitate forms. |
| B | Test 1: a dilute solution of $\text{HNO}_3$ is added. Test 2: a solution of $\text{AgNO}_3$ is added. | No visible reaction in either test. |
| C | Test 1: a solution of $\text{BaCl}_2$ is added. Test 2: a solution of HCl is added. | Test 1: a white precipitate forms. Test 2: no visible reaction. |
| D | A small sample of the solution was heated in the flame of a Bunsen burner. | The flame does not change colour. |

Identify the metal salt. Support your answer with at least ONE net ionic equation.
questions.answer:
The salt is **magnesium sulfate**, $\text{MgSO}_4$.

- The solution is colourless, so the cation is not $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (blue). The flame test (D) shows no colour, so the cation is not $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ (brick red) or $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (green), leaving $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.
- Sample A: $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$ (white precipitate), consistent with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.
- Magnesium hydroxide is insoluble, so the anion is not $\text{OH}^-$ (the salt dissolved).
- Sample B: no precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_3$ (in nitric acid), so there is no $\text{Cl}^-$.
- Sample C: $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)$ (white precipitate that does not dissolve in HCl), so the anion is $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$; it is not $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, since a carbonate would effervesce (and dissolve) with HCl.

questions.question:
Some properties of but-1-ene, 1-fluoropropane, propan-1-ol and ethanamide are shown in the table.

| Compound | Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | Solubility in water |
|---|---|---|
| But-1-ene | 56 | insoluble |
| 1-fluoropropane | 62 | slightly soluble |
| Propan-1-ol | 60 | soluble |
| Ethanamide | 59 | soluble |

Explain the different water solubilities of these compounds. Support your answer with at least ONE labelled diagram (describe the diagram).
questions.answer:
For a compound to dissolve in water, the attractions between the solute and water molecules must be strong enough to overcome the strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules. The compounds have similar molar masses, so their dispersion forces are similar and do not explain the differences; the difference is in the polarity and hydrogen bonding ability.

- **But-1-ene** is non-polar, so it can only form weak dispersion forces with water. These cannot overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so it is insoluble.
- **1-fluoropropane** has a polar C–F bond, so it can form dipole–dipole attractions with water, but it has no H attached to F/O/N and cannot donate hydrogen bonds (the C–F fluorine is a very weak hydrogen bond acceptor). These forces are only just strong enough to compete with water's hydrogen bonds, so it is only slightly soluble.
- **Propan-1-ol** has a polar $-$OH group which can form hydrogen bonds with water as both a donor ($\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{O}$ of water) and an acceptor (the oxygen lone pair with $\text{H}$ of water). The short non-polar propyl chain does not prevent it from dissolving, so it is soluble.
- **Ethanamide**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$, has a polar carbonyl group ($\text{C}=\text{O}$, an acceptor) and polar $\text{N}-\text{H}$ bonds (donors), so it forms many hydrogen bonds with water and is soluble.

*Diagram:* a molecule of propan-1-ol (or ethanamide) with its $\delta^-$ oxygen and $\delta^+$ hydrogen, and dotted lines labelled "hydrogen bond" to the $\delta^+$ H and $\delta^-$ O of neighbouring water molecules.

questions.question: The table shows common acid–base indicators and their pH ranges for colour change. Which of the indicators could be used to distinguish between solutions of $0.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide and $0.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: All six indicators could be used. $0.1$ M HCl is a strong acid with $pH=1$ and $0.1$ M NaOH is a strong base with $pH=13$, and each indicator has a different colour at these two pH values (which are outside the colour-change ranges): methyl orange is red at pH 1 and yellow at pH 13; bromothymol blue is yellow and blue; phenolphthalein is colourless and pink; litmus is red and blue; bromocresol green is yellow and blue; thymol blue is yellow and blue.

questions.question: The table shows common acid–base indicators and their pH ranges for colour change (thymol blue: pH 8.0–9.6, yellow to blue). A student claims that thymol blue can be used to distinguish between weak and strong bases. Assess this claim.
questions.answer: The claim is not valid in general. Thymol blue changes colour between pH 8.0 and 9.6, so it can only tell whether a solution is below pH 8.0 (yellow) or above 9.6 (blue); it cannot distinguish between solutions both above 9.6. The pH of a base depends on both its strength and its concentration. A concentrated weak base such as ammonia solution (pH above 9.6) would turn the indicator blue, the same as a strong base such as NaOH, so they could not be distinguished, and a very dilute strong base could have a pH below 8. The claim is only valid if the two bases have the same known concentration and one has a pH below 8.0 and the other above 9.6.

questions.question: The table shows common acid–base indicators and their pH ranges for colour change. Explain, using examples of titrations, why different titrations require the use of different acid–base indicators. Include a sketch of a titration curve in your answer.
questions.answer:
An indicator must change colour at the pH of the equivalence point, so that the end point (when the colour changes and titration stops) coincides with the equivalence point (when the moles of acid and base are in the ratio of the balanced equation). The pH at the equivalence point depends on the salt formed and so differs between titrations.

**Strong acid–strong base** (e.g. NaOH with HCl): the salt NaCl is neutral (neither $\text{Na}^+$ nor $\text{Cl}^-$ reacts with water), so the equivalence point is at pH 7, and the pH changes very rapidly from about 3 to 11 near it. An indicator that changes colour near 7, such as bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) or litmus, is suitable.

**Weak acid–strong base** (e.g. NaOH with $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$): the salt sodium ethanoate is basic because the ethanoate ion is a weak base ($\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{OH}^-$), so the equivalence point is at about pH 9, and the steep part of the curve lies between about 7 and 11. Phenolphthalein (8–9) is suitable, but methyl orange (3.1–4.4) would change colour long before the equivalence point.

(A sketch of pH against volume of base added for each titration is shown: the strong acid–strong base curve has a vertical section through pH 7, and the weak acid–strong base curve starts at a higher pH and has its steep section centred about pH 9.)

questions.question:
The flow chart shows reactions involving six different organic compounds, A–F. Compound A ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$), when heated with dilute sulfuric acid solution, gives compound B ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$) and compound C ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$). Compound B reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give compound D ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2\text{Na}(aq)$) and $\text{CO}_2(g)$. Compound C, heated with warm acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ solution, shows no reaction ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ recovered). Compound C heated with concentrated sulfuric acid gives compound E ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$), which reacts with hydrogen to give compound F ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$).

Draw the structural formula of compounds A–F and use the information provided to justify your answers.
questions.answer:
| Compound | Structural formula | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| A | $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$ (2-methylpropan-2-yl ethanoate, *tert*-butyl ethanoate) | An ester ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$) that is hydrolysed by dilute acid to a carboxylic acid (B) and an alcohol (C): $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2+\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ |
| B | $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{OH}$ (ethanoic acid) | Reacts with sodium carbonate to produce a sodium salt and $\text{CO}_2$ gas, as expected of a carboxylic acid of formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$ |
| C | $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OH}$ (2-methylpropan-2-ol) | An alcohol ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, formed by hydrolysis of the ester) that does not react with acidified permanganate, so it is a tertiary alcohol; the only four-carbon tertiary alcohol is 2-methylpropan-2-ol |
| D | $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}^-\ \text{Na}^+$ (sodium ethanoate) | The sodium salt of ethanoic acid (an ionic bond between $\text{Na}^+$ and the ethanoate ion) formed in the acid–carbonate reaction |
| E | $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ (2-methylpropene) | Dehydration of the alcohol C by concentrated sulfuric acid gives an alkene ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$) with the same branched carbon skeleton |
| F | $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$ (2-methylpropane) | Addition of hydrogen to alkene E gives the alkane $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ with the same branched skeleton |

questions.question:
Wines and other alcoholic drinks can spoil when the alcohol (ethanol) they contain oxidises to acetic acid (ethanoic acid). An acidity regulator, monosodium citrate, is often added to drinks to prevent the formation of acetic acid. The monosodium citrate does this by acting as a buffer. A citric acid/dihydrogen citrate ion buffer can be prepared from citric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$, and monosodium citrate, $\text{NaH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$.

Write an equation for the buffer system ($\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$ / $\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-$) containing citric acid and monosodium citrate.
questions.answer:
$$\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$
(or equivalently $\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$).

questions.question: A citric acid/dihydrogen citrate ion buffer ($\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$ / $\text{NaH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$) is most effective when it contains equal concentrations of both components. The buffer solution is prepared by mixing $100.0$ mL of citric acid solution with $100.0$ mL of monosodium citrate solution. The citric acid solution has a concentration of $0.200$ mol L$^{-1}$. Calculate the mass of monosodium citrate, $\text{NaH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$ ($M=214.1$ g mol$^{-1}$), that would need to be dissolved in $100.0$ mL of distilled water to make the most effective buffer solution.
questions.answer:
For the most effective buffer the two components have equal concentrations, so $c(\text{NaH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7)=0.200$ mol L$^{-1}$ in $100.0$ mL (the same volume as the citric acid).

$n=cV=0.200\times0.1000=0.0200$ mol.

$m=nM=0.0200\times214.106=4.28$ g.

questions.question: If a citric acid buffer was prepared to a pH of $3.5$, what would be the concentration of the hydroxide ion at $25.0^\circ$C?
questions.answer:
$[\text{H}^+]=10^{-3.5}=3.16\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. At $25^\circ$C, $K_w=1.0\times10^{-14}$:
$$[\text{OH}^-]=\frac{1.0\times10^{-14}}{3.16\times10^{-4}}=3\times10^{-11}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
(1 significant figure, since the pH has one decimal place; unrounded $3.16\times10^{-11}$).

questions.question: A citric acid/dihydrogen citrate buffer is prepared from citric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$, and monosodium citrate, $\text{NaH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$. Explain why only a small change in pH is observed in this buffer solution when a small amount of sodium hydroxide solution is added, compared to adding a similar amount of sodium hydroxide solution to a system that is not a buffer solution. Support your answer with at least ONE chemical equation.
questions.answer:
The buffer contains a weak acid ($\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7$) and its conjugate base ($\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-$) in large, similar amounts, in equilibrium: $\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$.

When a small amount of NaOH is added, the $\text{OH}^-$ ions react with and are removed by the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions (or by the citric acid): $\text{H}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}_7^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. The removal of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ shifts the equilibrium to the right (by Le Chatelier's principle), as more citric acid ionises and replaces the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ used. This slightly decreases the concentration of citric acid and slightly increases that of the citrate ion, but because both are present in large amounts their ratio, and so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ and the pH, change very little.

In a solution that is not a buffer (e.g. water or a solution of a strong acid or base only), there is no weak acid/conjugate base pair present to react with the added $\text{OH}^-$, so the added $\text{OH}^-$ directly increases $[\text{OH}^-]$ and the pH changes greatly.
